profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the developer platform telemetry workstream and the research tooling workstream for an internal pilot that studies decision-making in human-AI software engineering tasks, specifically code review and issue triage with an AI assistant in the loop. The pilot starts next week with two product squads, and the teams need to align on the interface between platform event producers and the research ingestion pipeline. The agenda is to confirm the target schema for the handoff, agree on what 'pilot-ready' means for Friday's milestone, clarify where the shared mapping artifact will be maintained, and line up Thursday's staging validation. The expected outcome is an apparently clean coordination plan: platform will finish the producer side, research will finalize the ingestion mapping, both will meet for validation, and a shared artifact will support the pilot handoff without either side sensing any major ambiguity.

members.name: Nadia Chen
members.expertise: developer analytics pipelines, experiment instrumentation, mixed-methods software engineering research
members.background: Nadia leads the embedded research engineering stream supporting a PhD study on human-AI collaboration in software engineering, and she has spent the last three years building event capture and analysis pipelines for code review, issue triage, and AI-assisted development workflows.
members.private_state: She needs the pilot to begin on time with analyzable data, wants to avoid reopening the study protocol and consent-related wording, and is trying to keep the integration lightweight enough that the platform team does not push back on extra custom work.
hidden_assumptions: When cross-team discussions mention the 'target schema,' the natural target is the normalized research datastore schema used for analysis, because that is the artifact the pilot ultimately depends on.
For a pilot, 'ready' primarily means the captured records are usable for the study's first-wave analyses, even if the surrounding operational hardening is still informal.
A 'shared mapping' is fundamentally a study artifact and therefore should live in the research workspace, with platform contributors adding notes rather than owning the source of truth.

When someone says 'staging validation,' the safest and most obvious approach is a controlled replay of synthetic sessions that preserve behavioral structure without involving realistic employee traces.
If the platform says they will expose the needed events, it is reasonable to assume downstream normalization and derived research fields are understood as part of the same handoff path.

members.name: Omar Singh
members.expertise: internal APIs, telemetry pipelines, service contracts, rollout coordination across engineering tools
members.background: Omar coordinates integrations across the code host, issue tracker, and internal AI assistant services, and he has previously led several telemetry launches where long-term interface ownership, operational reliability, and support boundaries mattered more than downstream analysis needs.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the integration within existing platform conventions, avoid creating support obligations his team has not staffed for, and ensure any pilot-facing handoff looks stable enough that product squads are not depending on ad hoc research infrastructure.
hidden_assumptions: When teams refer to the 'target schema,' the obvious target is the platform's unified event bus contract, because that is the shared interface other teams are expected to consume from.

For something to be 'ready' for a pilot, it should be operationally dependable in normal usage, including access setup, monitoring visibility, and at least minimal on-call clarity, not just data flowing once.

A 'shared mapping' tied to an interface belongs with the producing system's contract material, so the authoritative version should live in the platform repo or schema registry even if others link to it.
When someone proposes 'staging validation,' the standard assumption is the normal staging stack with connected services and scrubbed-realistic traffic patterns, not a custom replay harness.
If a downstream team needs normalized or derived fields, that is normally their transformation layer; producer-side contracts should stay close to raw emitted events unless explicitly renegotiated.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to aligning on 'the target schema' and finishing 'the mapping to the target' as if they mean the same endpoint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the normalized research-facing schema in the analysis datastore, where raw tool events are transformed into study constructs such as actor_role, suggestion_source, decision_outcome, and confidence_marker.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the platform's unified event bus contract that producers publish to, where emitted events remain close to service-native telemetry and downstream consumers perform their own normalization.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional telemetry work, both layers are real and both are often casually called 'the schema,' so each person hears the other's phrasing as referring to their own layer in the same pipeline rather than as naming a different handoff endpoint.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the integration should be 'pilot-ready by Friday' for the core tools.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks pilot-ready means the core tools are producing data that reaches the research pipeline with enough completeness and consistency to support the first week of planned analyses, even if operational processes are still lightweight.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks pilot-ready means the same core tools are integrated in a way that is operationally supportable in ordinary use, including basic monitoring, access readiness, and clear ownership for handling issues during the pilot.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing the same tools and same deadline, so the divergence is not about scope but about the quality threshold for the word 'ready'—a second-order assumption that usually stays implicit because each standard feels obviously appropriate for a pilot.

misalignment_points.topic: Where the shared mapping lives and who owns it
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Nadia will 'update the shared mapping' and Omar will 'link to it' after validation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the shared mapping is the Confluence page in the research workspace that documents how platform fields map into the study's canonical constructs, and that this page is the practical source of truth for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the shared mapping is the interface documentation entry in the platform schema registry or API repo, with any research page being only a consumer-side reference or mirror.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both organizations commonly use mirrored documentation, and the phrase 'the shared mapping' sounds singular and established; because neither expects ownership location itself to be contentious, they do not realize they are presupposing different authoritative artifacts.

misalignment_points.topic: How staging validation will be run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'do staging validation on Thursday' before the handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a controlled replay of a curated synthetic developer-AI session through the ingestion path so the research team can verify event completeness and semantic reconstructability against the study protocol.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a standard staging integration check using the normal connected services, ordinary smoke-test flows, and the platform's usual validation steps for contract and service health.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both methods are legitimate and routine within their own workstreams, and 'staging validation' sounds sufficiently standard that neither participant feels a need to unpack the exact mechanics during a coordination-focused meeting.
